justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near the current market price and gradually increasing. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 76.2 is essentially anchored to the last observed price level, with only minimal expected movement since most short-term price action tends to mean-revert or drift very slightly. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 76.8 reflects a small positive drift assumption, consistent with the historical tendency of this type of asset to trend modestly upward over short to medium windows when no major catalysts are imminent. At the one-month horizon, the estimate climbs to 78.0, compounding that drift assumption while also incorporating a slightly higher expected return premium for the longer holding period. In all three cases, the point estimates are conservative and do not assume any dramatic directional moves.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably with time horizon, reflecting the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 2.7 points because there is limited time for new information to arrive and compound. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 5.75 points, accounting for several potential trading sessions and the possibility of moderate news events. At one month, the interval spans about 26 points total, reflecting the reality that over four weeks, macroeconomic data, earnings surprises, geopolitical developments, or shifts in market sentiment can move prices substantially in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, an unexpected policy shift from a central bank, or a broad risk-off episode in equity or commodity markets could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. Liquidity crunches or forced selling by large participants could also create sharp, rapid dislocations that exceed the one-day interval. On the upside, a strong positive surprise in underlying fundamentals, a short squeeze dynamic, or a broader risk-on rally could push prices comfortably above the upper bounds.

It is worth noting that my intervals are calibrated at the 90% confidence level, meaning I am explicitly acknowledging roughly a one-in-ten chance that the actual outcome falls outside these ranges. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that extreme outcomes happen more frequently than a simple normal distribution would suggest, so users should treat these intervals as reasonable planning bounds rather than hard limits. Model error in my drift and volatility assumptions also contributes additional uncertainty that is difficult to fully quantify.
